detroit.intro: Detroit's old trees start at Historic Elmwood Cemetery on the east side, which in 2015 became the first certified arboretum in the city. The cemetery calls a bur oak in its Bloody Run valley the oldest tree on the grounds, at about 280 years. Section O holds what it says is Michigan's second largest sweet gum, last measured in 2016. The grounds run to about 86 acres, so take the free tree tour maps, and check opening hours before you go.
detroit.meta_description: Detroit's oldest mapped tree is a bur oak of about 280 years in Elmwood Cemetery, which also holds Michigan's second largest sweet gum.
detroit.question_meta: Detroit's oldest mapped tree is the bur oak in Historic Elmwood Cemetery, about 280 years old by the cemetery's own figure.
detroit.question_answer: The oldest tree we map in Detroit is a Bur Oak (Quercus macrocarpa) in the Bloody Run valley of Historic Elmwood Cemetery, about 280 years old. That figure comes from the cemetery itself, which owns the ground and names it the oldest tree in its arboretum; nobody else has published one.
detroit.question_context: If the cemetery's number holds, the oak has been growing since about the 1740s. Elmwood gained Level I ArbNet arboretum status in 2015, the first in Detroit, and posts self-guided tree tour maps on its site. The trouble is finding the trunk. The cemetery covers about 86 acres, we have no coordinate for this oak yet, and its tour maps are the place to look, along with the office at 1200 Elmwood Avenue. The other tree worth the walk is a sweet gum in Section O, near a junction of four streets, entered in the Michigan Big Tree Register as number 657. The register measured it in November 2016 at 253 centimetres round and 23.5 metres tall, and the cemetery calls it the second largest of its species in Michigan. Nobody has published an age for that one. Photographs on the arboretum page date from Arbor Day 2025, though none can be matched to the oak. If you have stood under either tree, tell us exactly where, and confirm opening hours with the office before you set out.

faq.q: How old is the Elmwood Cemetery bur oak?
faq.a: About 280 years, according to Historic Elmwood Cemetery, which owns the ground. No ring count or second estimate has been published.

faq.q: Can you visit Elmwood Cemetery's trees for free?
faq.a: Yes, the grounds are open to visitors and the cemetery posts free self-guided tree tour maps. Confirm opening hours with the office first.

faq.q: Where in the cemetery is the big sweet gum?
faq.a: In Section O, near a junction of four streets. The Michigan Big Tree Register lists it as number 657, and its published coordinates are too rounded to use.

ann-arbor.intro: Ann Arbor measures its trees and publishes the scores. Its Champion Tree Map names a chinkapin oak in Wurster Park as the largest of its species in Michigan and the biggest tree of any species in town by girth, 549 centimetres round. In West Park a bur oak has a crown wider than the tree is tall, and a northern red oak stands at the Miller Avenue entrance about 120 metres away. All three stand in free city parks, and nobody has published an age for any of them.
ann-arbor.meta_description: Ann Arbor's champion oaks: Michigan's largest chinkapin in Wurster Park, and a West Park bur oak with a crown wider than it is tall.
ann-arbor.question_meta: No age is published for Ann Arbor's great trees. The biggest is the Wurster Park chinkapin oak, 549 cm round and Michigan's largest.
ann-arbor.question_answer: No tree we map in Ann Arbor has a published age, so nobody can honestly name the oldest. The biggest is the Chinkapin Oak (Quercus muehlenbergii) in Wurster Park, the largest of its species in Michigan and, at 549 centimetres round, the largest tree of any species in the city by girth.
ann-arbor.question_context: What Ann Arbor has instead of dates is a scoreboard. The city's Champion Tree Map, verified by the city itself, gives the Wurster Park oak 359.5 points, from a circumference of 549 centimetres, a height of 35.7 metres and a crown of 106 feet. The Michigan Big Tree Register measured the same trunk in 2016 at 215 inches round but put the height at 110 feet against the city's 117, so treat the height as a range. You will find it just inside the woods at the south-west corner of the park, at 525 W Madison Street. West Park, near downtown, holds two more champions from the same map. A bur oak in the middle of the park, east of the bandshell, scored 322.2, with a trunk 520 centimetres round and a crown of 121 feet on a height of 87.2. The northern red oak at the Miller Avenue entrance scored 251.9. Those West Park figures date from 2020, and we have found no independent report since. If you know the age of any of these oaks, tell us.

faq.q: What is the biggest tree in Ann Arbor?
faq.a: By girth, the chinkapin oak in Wurster Park, 549 centimetres round. The city's park page also names it the largest chinkapin oak in Michigan.

faq.q: Where exactly is the Wurster Park oak?
faq.a: Just inside the woods at the park's south-west corner. The park is at 525 W Madison Street in the Old West Side and is free.

faq.q: How are Ann Arbor's champion trees chosen?
faq.a: The city scores them on its Champion Tree Map, which gives each tree a points total alongside its circumference, height and crown spread. A champion holds its title for two years after verification.

lansing.intro: Lansing's two old trees are both in East Lansing, on the Michigan State University campus about five kilometres east of downtown. The Resilient Oak on the Campus Oval gave up 347 annual rings after a 2016 storm, and its curator puts it at 375 to 400 years. In Beal Botanical Garden stands a dawn redwood planted in 1954, a species thought extinct until the 1940s, with a lightning arrestor of its own. Both are free to visit and stops on the campus tree tour.
lansing.meta_description: East Lansing's Resilient Oak, a white oak with 347 counted rings and a 375 to 400 year estimate, on the Michigan State University campus.
lansing.question_meta: The Lansing area's oldest mapped tree is the Resilient Oak in East Lansing, 347 rings counted, estimated at 375 to 400 years.
lansing.question_answer: The oldest tree we map around Lansing is the Resilient Oak, a White Oak (Quercus alba) on the Michigan State University campus in East Lansing. A section above the base showed 347 annual rings after a storm in 2016, and the campus arboretum's curator estimates the whole tree at 375 to 400 years.
lansing.question_context: It is a rare thing to have counted rings on a tree you can still go and see. The storm of 8 July 2016 blew the oak over, and a 20-foot section above the base gave up its rings. The curator's 375 to 400 allows for slow growth under shade. The university describes the tree as a survivor of the forest that covered this ground before 1855. It was topped about a century ago, an operation in the college's own 1915 history that left a metal cap, and it lost roots to a sidewalk. It was named in the autumn of 2017. What remains is a hollow trunk at the edge of the path, near Beaumont Tower, stop 8 on the campus tree tour, and reports from 2024 and 2025 say it keeps growing. Other old oaks stand around the Oval, and the tour suspects they are survivors too, but none has dated rings. A short walk west, in Beal Botanical Garden, the dawn redwood planted in 1954 is the first stop on the same tour. East Lansing lies about five kilometres east of downtown Lansing.

faq.q: How do we know the age of the Resilient Oak?
faq.a: After it blew over in 2016, a 20-foot section above the base showed 347 annual rings. The curator's estimate of 375 to 400 years allows for slow growth in shade.

faq.q: Is the Resilient Oak in Lansing or East Lansing?
faq.a: East Lansing, on the Michigan State University campus near Beaumont Tower, about five kilometres east of downtown Lansing.

faq.q: Why does the dawn redwood at Beal Garden have a lightning arrestor?
faq.a: Lightning struck it in the 1990s. An arrestor was fitted in October 2012, and in 2017 the university said more than 20 feet would come off the top because of decay from the lightning crack.

cleveland.intro: Cleveland's most famous tree is young, and its oldest are a matter of belief. The Edgewater willow, about 70 years old, stands on lakefront fill from the 1950s and gets proposed under. Across town, Lake View Cemetery looks after seven Moses Cleaveland trees, believed by a 1946 survey to predate 1796. Here you can see a tulip tree on Chapel Road, a white oak that looks out of Sleepy Hollow, a sycamore with camouflage bark and a black oak held up with cables. All are free to visit.
cleveland.meta_description: Cleveland's Edgewater willow and the Moses Cleaveland trees of Lake View Cemetery, believed by a 1946 survey to predate 1796.
cleveland.question_meta: Cleveland's oldest trees are the Moses Cleaveland trees of Lake View Cemetery, believed by a 1946 survey to predate 1796; none has a ring count.
cleveland.question_answer: Cleveland's oldest mapped trees are the Moses Cleaveland trees of Lake View Cemetery, believed to be over 230 years old. That is the belief of a 1946 survey, not a ring count, and none can be ranked against the others. The largest tulip tree of the group, on Chapel Road, stands for them here.
cleveland.question_context: The Early Settlers Association went looking in 1946 for trees that had been standing before 1796, and it qualified them by the width of the trunk. A later survey in 1971 came back and measured again, which is why we can say the Chapel Road tulip tree went from 37 inches across to 39 and the Section 8 white oak from 36 to 40. Lake View counts seven of these trees today. The two tallest are tulip trees in Sections 1 and 6, the sycamore with camouflage bark is in Section 5a, and the black oak held up by cables and brace rods is in Section 14. A larger white oak grows in Section 42, for which we have no figures. Take the cemetery's keyed map, because sections are the real address and our pins mark Wade Memorial Chapel, not the trunks. The city's best-known tree is another matter altogether. The willow at Edgewater Beach dates only to about 1953 to 1958, on land made in the 1950s from the straightening of the Cuyahoga River.

faq.q: What is a Moses Cleaveland tree?
faq.a: A tree believed to have been standing before 1796, listed by a survey of 1946 that chose them by trunk diameter. The age is the survey's belief; no rings were counted.

faq.q: How old is the Edgewater weeping willow?
faq.a: About 70 years. A Metroparks historian dates it to roughly 1953 to 1958, on land filled in during the 1950s.

faq.q: How do you find the trees in Lake View Cemetery?
faq.a: By section number. The cemetery publishes a keyed map, and each of these trees has its own section, from 1 or 6 for the tulip tree to 14 for the black oak.

sacramento.intro: Both of Sacramento's trees here stand around the State Capitol, and they could hardly differ more. On the north-east lawn is a coast redwood grown from a seed carried around the moon on Apollo 14 and planted in 1976, the city's only Moon Tree. On the west front, ten Himalayan cedars line the lawn, several from an original planting of 1872, and one of them is the largest deodar in California. The Capitol's guide does not say which. Capitol Park is free and open daily.
sacramento.meta_description: Capitol Park's Moon Tree, a redwood whose seed went round the moon on Apollo 14, and the deodar cedars planted at Sacramento's Capitol from 1872.
sacramento.question_meta: Sacramento's oldest mapped trees are the deodar cedars on the Capitol's west front, several planted in 1872, over 150 years ago.
sacramento.question_answer: Sacramento's oldest mapped trees are the Himalayan Cedars (Cedrus deodara) on the west side of the State Capitol, several of them from an original twelve planted in 1872, which makes them more than 150 years old. The State Capitol Museum's guide does not say which of the ten standing today date from that planting.
sacramento.question_context: The same guide says one of the cedars is California's largest deodar, drawing on the California Big Trees Registry, and again declines to say which. You can take them as a set on the lawn at the west entrance. The building has a younger and stranger neighbour on its north-east side. In 1971 Apollo 14 carried tree seeds around the moon, and this coast redwood grew from one of them, collected near Soquel in 1966. It was planted in April 1976 at about two feet tall, and NASA's 2024 update has it near 120 feet. It is the city's only Moon Tree and one of seven in California. Capitol Park has had a difficult few years, as the Capitol Annex project put dozens of its trees at risk, 20 to 30 by the state's estimate and up to 100 by advocates' count. We have found no report of a cedar being removed, and our evidence that the Moon Tree still stands runs to 2024. Annex works may fence off some paths, so allow time to walk round.

faq.q: Where is the Moon Tree in Sacramento?
faq.a: On the lawn at the north-east corner of the California State Capitol, beside the security pavilion near 10th and L Streets.

faq.q: Which cedar at the Capitol is the state champion?
faq.a: The Capitol's tree guide says one of the ten on the west front is California's largest deodar, without saying which.

faq.q: Is the Moon Tree still alive?
faq.a: NASA described it as standing in a 2024 update, the latest evidence we have. A 2023 report said it was being protected during the Capitol Annex works.

santa-cruz.intro: Santa Cruz's big redwoods are in Felton, about ten kilometres north of town, on the short Redwood Grove loop in Henry Cowell Redwoods State Park. Stop 7 is The Giant, 270 feet tall and over 17 feet wide by the park's own guide. Stop 8 is the Fremont Tree, a burnt-out, still-living redwood you can step inside, where a general may or may not have spent a night in 1846. He refused to confirm it. The walk is flat, and a day-use fee applies.
santa-cruz.meta_description: The Giant and the hollow Fremont Tree, two old-growth coast redwoods on the Redwood Grove loop at Henry Cowell park in Felton, near Santa Cruz.
santa-cruz.question_meta: The oldest tree we map near Santa Cruz is likely The Giant, a Felton coast redwood; estimates of 1,200 to 1,800 years are a hedge.
santa-cruz.question_answer: The oldest tree we map near Santa Cruz is probably The Giant, a Coast Redwood (Sequoia sempervirens) at stop 7 of the Redwood Grove loop in Henry Cowell Redwoods State Park, Felton. A roughly 1,500-year figure comes from a visitor's caption, and nothing official dates this trunk; 1,200 to 1,800 years is a hedge.
santa-cruz.question_context: California State Parks gives The Giant two numbers in its trail guide, 270 feet tall and more than 17 feet wide, and leaves its age alone. The guide's only remark on age is general, that a mature redwood can pass 2,000 years. A visitor's dated photograph from 2026 is captioned at roughly 1,500 years and about 277 feet. A figure of 1,200 to 1,600 years has also been attributed to State Parks for the park's tallest redwood, but we have not seen the original. The next stop on the loop is the Fremont Tree, burnt out and hollow and still alive, with a base you can step into. General John C. Fremont reportedly slept in it in 1846, and when he was asked about that in 1888, his reply was that it made a great story and should stand. The grove was Santa Cruz County Big Trees Park before it became a state park in 1953, after the Cowell family gave the land. Felton is about ten kilometres north of Santa Cruz, the loop is short and flat, and the park charges a day-use fee.

faq.q: How tall is The Giant at Henry Cowell?
faq.a: The State Parks trail guide gives 270 feet, with a trunk more than 17 feet wide. A visitor's caption from 2026 says about 277 feet.

faq.q: Did Fremont really sleep in the Fremont Tree?
faq.a: He reportedly did in 1846. Asked in 1888, he said it makes a great story and to let it stand, which is not a yes.

faq.q: Do you have to pay to see these redwoods?
faq.a: Yes, Henry Cowell Redwoods State Park charges a day-use fee. Check parks.ca.gov for current hours.
